mt_waltz_formation_the.blurb: A fin-shaped gneiss formation on the east bank of the Gallatin River, inside Gallatin Canyon south of Bozeman. The rock steps up in three tiers that point at the water, and quality changes from one tier to the next. Most of the 21 routes are trad, with a few bolted lines, and grades run from 5.7 up into the 5.13 range, with the bulk between 5.10 and 5.12. One long, moderate line brings steady traffic, so expect company. The face is mostly sunny, which makes mornings or evenings the better choice in midsummer. A short climbers' path climbs from the riverside trail to the base.

mt_main_cliff.blurb: The biggest and most varied wall in a limestone cluster beside a Forest Service campground in Gallatin Canyon, at roughly 6,400 feet. Nearly all of its 21 routes are bolted sport lines, with a single top rope. Grades start easy and reach 5.10, with most falling between 5.8 and 5.10. Expect a mix of steep, short, long and slabby pitches on rock of uneven quality, with a cave in the middle of the tallest section. Most lines are short, and one or two are noticeably longer. A fairly easy trail walk leads up to the base.

mt_7_11_crag.blurb: A compact cliff in the Allenspur group of Paradise Valley, a few miles south of Livingston, looking down on the Yellowstone River. Climbing is mostly bolted sport, with a couple of trad lines and one top rope, from 5.6 to low 5.12 and most of it between 5.9 and 5.11. The dolomitic limestone is solid. The wall faces southwest, so summer afternoons can run hot, though valley wind often takes the edge off; an early start helps with both heat and people. It is a quick walk in and usually quieter than the busy Gallatin Canyon crags.
mt_7_11_crag.parking_note: Leave the car at the fishing access by Carter's Bridge, off East River Road, and walk along the road to the climbers' trail.

mt_gallatin_tower.blurb: The signature gneiss tower on the highway side of Gallatin Canyon, and one of the busiest spots in the canyon. Most of the 21 routes are trad, packed with classics and some of the better cracks around, including two- and three-pitch lines, plus a handful of bolted routes. Grades run from 5.6 up to the 5.13 range, spread fairly evenly through 5.8 to 5.12. The tower looks east and picks up early light, so mornings are warm and later hours cooler. Roadside parking puts you close to the base.
mt_gallatin_tower.parking_note: Use the dirt pullout right beside the highway, almost directly below the tower, about nine miles into the canyon on the right when driving south.

mt_main_wall.blurb: The busiest wall in Lost Horse Canyon, in the Bitterroot Valley south of Hamilton. All 20 routes are trad, mostly cracks on clean, solid granite, in a canyon known for some of the state's best crack climbing. Grades run from 5.8 to 5.11 with a fairly even spread, including both short pitches and longer multi-pitch lines. It makes a good objective for a party with a full rack and a taste for jamming.

mt_porcelain_wall.blurb: A large, pale limestone wall set among trees above the Boulder River at Natural Bridge and Falls, near Big Timber. All 20 routes are bolted sport lines, from 5.10 to 5.12, weighted toward 5.11 and 5.12. The rock is steep by Montana standards and favors small edges. Trees shade parts of the base, and the spot sees few people. Getting there means scrambling through a rock corridor into the river basin, then crossing scree and a short wooded rise. Expect the first few moves off the ground to be the awkward part.

nv_cactus_joes.blurb: A small south-facing sport crag in the Mount Potosi area of southern Nevada, near the turnoff for Potosi Canyon at roughly 5,500 feet. About 29 bolted routes cover 5.7 to the 5.13 range, concentrated at 5.10 and 5.11, with a few easier and a few harder. Sun hits the wall all day, which suits cool weather and is miserable in heat. It is not a destination crag, but it fills a day or two nicely.
